current_note_text: Perseus Horse] MALONE (ed. 1790) is the first editor to remark on this association of Perseus and Pegasus. He thought that Sh. was following the Recuyell (ed. But he then adduces evidence to prove that authorities before Sh. had mounted Perseus on a horse. “Boccaccio, in his Genealogia Deorum, lib. xii. c. 25, has quoted Lactantius as saying, that when Perseus undertook his expedition against Gorgon, at the instance of king Polydectus, he was accompanied by the winged horse Pegasus. ... Boccaccio adds that others were of opinion that he had a ship called Pegasus. The liberties which the old French translators of Ovid’s Metamorphoses have taken, and their interpolations, are unaccountable. Some have caused Perseus at the instant of his birth to bestride Pegasus, and travel away to Helicon. There is in fact no reason. Ulysses addresses Agamemnon and Nestor; the parenthesis is a vocative; and the distinction between the greatness of the one and the wisdom of the other has been clearly made in lines 66-67. By omitting the comma after "great" Dyce and Hudson destroy the sense and the proper elocution. 79-80. These lines are based upon Chapman's translation of the Iliad. A fairly literal translation of Homer's passage is, "only Thersites chattered on, the uncontrolled of speech, whose mind was full of words many and disorderly" (Lang, Leaf, & Myers, Iliad, 1883, p. 28). Chapman based his verse translation of these lines upon the Latin verse translation found in Spondanus (Homeri quæ extant omnia, Basle, 1582, p. 33), the edition from which he is known to have translated: "Thersites adhuc solus immoderate verbosus crocitabat Qui verba mentibus suis inornataq; multa; sciebat." Chapman translates this as: "Thersites sole except, A man of tongue, whose rauenlike voice, a tuneles iarring kept, Who in his ranke minde coppy had of vnregarded wordes" (ed. 1598, sig. Evi).
